newsitem.title: GREECE: ECU/GRD VOLATILITY QUESTIONS HARD DRACHMA - DEUTSCHE.
newsitem.headline: ECU/GRD VOLATILITY QUESTIONS HARD DRACHMA - DEUTSCHE.

text.p: The hands-off approach by the Bank of Greece to the weakening of the drachma versus the ecu beyond the 310 level has raised doubts about the hard drachma policy, said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in its weekly global forex strategy report.

"The fact that the central bank has not stepped in to reverse the weakening of the ecu/drachma beyond 310 raises confusion whether this is part of the declared intention of the Bank of Greece to inject volatility with the aim to discourage speculative capital inflows or whether the authorities are revising and/or modifying their hard drachma policy," it said.

Bank of Greece governor Lucas Papademos has said recently that foreign exchange policy would remain anti-inflationary in 1997 and called for structural reforms and faster fiscal consolidation to take the convergence burden off the shoulders of monetary and forex policy.

The hard drachma policy has been one of the main anti-inflationary policy tools. The drachma slipped just 1.0 percent against the ecu in 1996 and 3.0 percent in 1995, in line with the central bank's targets.
The central bank has announced that it wants to keep the drachma broadly stable against the currencies that make up the ecu in 1997.

The drachma's PPP-based overvaluation was bound to get worse in light of persistent inflation differentials -- in excess of 400 basis points -- between Greece and its other EU partners, Deutsche said.

The overvaluation coupled with prospective ERM membership two years prior to EMU entry and current account deficits close to 4.0 percent of GDP made a medium-term drachma depreciation necessary, it added.
The report echoed senior bankers at local branches of foreign banks who commented that the fast drop in inflation made it easier for the central bank to relax its hard drachma policy.
Headline CPI inflation fell to 6.0 percent year-on-year in March from 6.6 percent in February.
Deutsche Morgan also recommended that investors "stay out of the drachma market for now," anticipating cross-European shock-waves from the French elections.
"We expect high-yielders to come under some pressure as we are approaching French elections and part of it will spill over to the drachma," a Deutsche Morgan Grenfell trader told Reuters.
The first round of French legislative elections is to be held in late May and the run-off in early June.

"French elections carry potentially far-reaching implications for EMU and European markets in general and will create volatility and increased mark demand," the report said. "We have cut our one-month $/mark forecast to 1.73 from 1.75."
